entry.title: What is happening?
entry.intro: Pick the closest one. You do not need to know technical words. Your bank fraud line stays at the top of every screen.

options.text: My device or files are locked
Someone accessed my email or account
I paid after bank details changed
I was asked to pay or change bank details, and I have not paid
It looks like an ordinary payment problem

clarify.title: One quick question
clarify.intro: We could not tell what happened from your description. Your bank fraud line stays at the top of every screen.
clarify.question: Which is closest to what is happening?

options.text: Money has been paid out, or is missing
My files or device are locked, or someone wants money to unlock them
Someone may have got into my email or an account
I got a suspicious message or link, and nothing has been paid or locked

payment_diversion.title: Possible payment diversion
payment_diversion.summary: Money may have been paid to a criminal after banking details changed. Act on step one now.

steps.title: Call your bank's fraud line now
steps.why: Only your bank can try to stop or recall the payment. Minutes count.
do: Choose your bank and call its official fraud line.
Say: I made a payment to a fraudulent account. Please try to stop or recall it.
Write down the reference number.

steps.title: Confirm with your supplier on a number you already had
steps.why: Do not reply to the suspicious email or call a number in it.
do: Use a number from an old invoice, your contacts or the supplier's official website.
Ask if they genuinely changed their banking details.

steps.title: Check your mailbox
steps.why: Criminals may hide or forward messages so they can watch payment conversations.
do: Look for forwarding and inbox rules you did not create.
Check recent sign-ins and change your password from a clean device.
Turn on two-step verification.

steps.title: Keep the evidence
steps.why: Your bank, SAPS and insurer may ask for the message and proof of payment.
do: Do not delete the email or message.
Save the proof of payment and screenshots.
Next you can fingerprint your files on this phone and make an incident pack.

mailbox_compromise.title: Possible hacked mailbox
mailbox_compromise.summary: Lock the mailbox before it is used to send fraudulent invoices.
mailbox_compromise.orgNote: If this is a work account at a larger organisation, tell your IT or security team first and follow their instructions. Do not change company systems on your own.

steps.title: Lock the account
do: Change the password from a clean device.
Turn on two-step verification and sign out other sessions.

steps.title: Remove unknown rules
steps.why: Forwarding rules can keep leaking email after a password change.
do: Remove rules and forwarding you did not create.
Keep screenshots for IT support.

suspicious_message.title: Suspicious message — no money moved
suspicious_message.summary: Good: you may be able to stop the scam before money leaves.

steps.title: Don't pay, click or reply
steps.why: A changed-bank-details message is a common payment-diversion tactic.
do: Do not change any banking details from the message.
Confirm the request on a trusted number.

ransomware_suspected.title: Possible ransomware: locked files or a demand for money
ransomware_suspected.summary: Files or a computer may be locked and someone may be demanding money. Stop it spreading, do not pay yet, and get a trusted specialist. Mgadi cannot unlock files or remove malware.
ransomware_suspected.orgNote: If you work for a larger organisation, call your IT or security team first and follow their instructions. Do not change company systems on your own.

steps.title: Look at what you can see, without clicking anything
steps.why: Ransomware often shows a message that demands money, or stops your files from opening. Other problems can look similar, so look first.
do: Look at the screen: is there a message that demands money or gives a deadline?
Notice whether your files have strange new endings or will not open.
Take a photo of the screen with another phone. Do not click anything in the message.
steps.done: I've looked and noted what I see

steps.title: Disconnect the affected computer from the network
steps.why: This can stop locked files from spreading to other computers and shared drives.
do: Unplug the network cable, or turn off Wi-Fi on the affected computer.
Disconnect any backup or shared drive that is plugged into it.
Do not switch it off unless you cannot disconnect it. Switching off can erase clues. If you had to, tell your specialist.
Leave everything as it is. Do not delete, rename or reinstall anything.

steps.title: Do not pay, and do not reply to the attackers yet
steps.why: Paying does not guarantee your files come back, and attackers may demand more. Official guidance does not recommend paying.
do: Do not pay or send cryptocurrency until a specialist has advised you.
Do not download or run any decryptor, cleaner or recovery tool from the message, an advert or a search result.
If you have already sent money from a bank account, use the red Bank fraud line button now and tell your bank.

steps.title: Get a trusted specialist, using a different device
steps.why: Locked files need an expert to check what happened and what can be saved. Use a phone or a computer that is not connected to the affected network.
do: Call your IT support, managed IT provider or a cybersecurity specialist you already know. Use a phone call, not email from the affected computer.
If you work for a larger organisation, tell your IT or security team first and follow their instructions. Do not change company systems on your own.
If you have cyber insurance, check your policy and ask your insurer what they need from you, and when.
Be careful with strangers who offer to fix it and ask for access or passwords. Criminals pose as helpers.

steps.title: Keep the information a specialist will need
steps.why: A responder can work faster if the clues are not lost.
do: Keep the photo of the message. Do not contact any email address or wallet details it shows.
Write down when you first noticed it, which computer, and what you did.
Do not delete files, empty the recycle bin or reinstall the system.
Do not upload your private files anywhere. Your specialist will tell you what, if anything, to share.

steps.title: Protect your backups
steps.why: A clean backup kept apart from the computer is often the safest way back. A backup that also gets locked cannot help.
do: Do not plug a backup drive into the affected computer.
Disconnect any online backup that is connected to the affected network, and tell your specialist.
Do not restore anything until your specialist says it is safe. Restoring onto an infected computer can lock it again.
Write down where your backups are and when the last good one was made.

steps.title: Prepare a handoff and know your next steps
steps.why: A short summary saves time for your specialist, the police, your insurer and your bank.
do: Next, make an incident pack on this phone. It holds only what you tell Mgadi, and you choose what goes in.

Report the crime to the South African Police Service. Ask your specialist about other duties. If personal information may have been exposed, they can advise whether the Information Regulator and the people affected must be told.
Ask your specialist whether a free decryption tool may exist for your case. For many kinds of ransomware none exists, so never count on one.

not_cyber.title: This may not be a cyber incident
not_cyber.summary: It sounds like a normal payment or admin problem, but stay cautious.

steps.title: Double-check before you relax
steps.why: Scams can look like an ordinary late payment.
do: If details changed, start again and treat it as suspicious.
If money left for an unfamiliar account, call your bank.

unsure.title: Let's be safe
unsure.summary: We could not tell what happened. Take the safest steps while you find out.

steps.title: If money may have moved, call your bank now
steps.why: The bank may be able to stop the payment. If no money has moved, you can continue.
do: Choose your bank below and call its official fraud number.
Only press the button when you have actually called.

steps.title: Pause before you pay or change anything
steps.why: Criminals rely on speed. A short check can stop a loss.
do: Do not pay, or change a supplier's banking details, until you have checked.
Phone the supplier on a number you already had, not one from the message.
Keep the message; you can add it to an incident pack.
